utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that would now be a convenient moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume a little after five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal, please, with -- have you kept the document open or not? It's tab 22. All right. Can we deal, then, please, with the reference. You've told us about -- that the briefing by 1. Can we deal then with the next part? Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, point b --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think we hadn't concluded a, had we? "ECMM insisted that all wounded and" --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That all wounded and ill people as medical crew should be transported (by the agreement) and that all prisoners of war must be treated by Geneva Convention. ICRC should provide and check the list of all people in hospital and in convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's deal with the convoy. We can see clearly the numbers given there. I don't want to deal with that to any great extent.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so it's b: "Convoy consists of 10 army ambulances, each for four patients, four coaches, for light patients, light wounded patients, and one ambulance, civil ambulance for a small girl."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. But I would like to deal with c, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, could we deal with the first part, Vukovar, c, the symbol seems to mean approximately --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two hours waiting in a centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Demining." Now, I would like you to just deal with this, if I may. Firstly, why do you have, "Demining?"

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was a question, if it was a demining or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that it is demining. We were not monitor observed that, so if I have writing that, I have to stress that I was told that it was demine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I would like you to look then at a video, which is our 65 ter 315 -- sorry, my apologies, 314. It should start at the time 1731, and I hope, continue to 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court, this is the disagreement on the bridge with Nicholas Borsinger and Sljivancanin, and this particular version has got subtitles which will run with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just actually ask that we stop, because we clearly haven't got the sound. Can we just clarify to see if there is a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the best way of dealing with this, if I may suggest, is as follows. The sound normally travels with this CD without any difficulty, I don't know why it's missing. Perhaps if we can play it, the transcript is there anyway, what is actually being said, and then there is another one that I wish to play following that. So it -- I would have thought there is no reason at all why we can't continue. So if we could take it back to the beginning, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with that video, we're trying to get the sound sorted out, there may be a technical problem. But this is clearly on the bridge on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, is it right that you saw this occurring?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, where were you actually located when you saw this occurring?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were located in the beginning of -- of this whole column. It's -- it means we were the fourth or fifth car in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going to try and do, we have another video, it's actually the same as this video, but it extends for approximately three or four more seconds, and I'm going to try and pan the video right around, or play the video, so that we can see back down the column. So let us see if we can try and work that. The exhibit number is Exhibit 283. Now can that be played, please, so that it concludes at the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just freeze that for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the same location, the difference here is the video has continued on round and is looking back down the road, and we can see the door of ICRC vehicle, and then we can see various vehicles lined up behind with a large building on the right. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, are you able to remember -- clearly the ICRC vehicle is at the bridge, but whereabouts are you located in relation to that? Behind the ICRC vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really. I remember the place where we were staying for a -- for this time, and it's -- it was near this -- it was near this brown building on the right side of the road. On the opposite side there is a Hotel Danube, so I remember the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were somewhere around there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just play this to the end so that we can just finalise the part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just move on? You've told us about two hours waiting in the centre. And then there is the following: "In the totally destroyed town." Can you read that part, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. "In the totally destroyed town, -- bands of and Serbian volunteers and Territorial Defence units which were firing and searching usable things in ruins. Some of them were drunk and a lot of aggressive smell of dead bodies, some bodies were visible, some were into ruins."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think you've got here the reference to the conflict between 1. Now, you've got 1 as Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I remember that it was Major Sljivancanin, and it's a mistake, I can't explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you refer to, if we look at the top of that page that we're looking at, 1402, we can see that there is a briefing by 1. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And 1, by way of your index, was Pavkovic. So are you able to assist whether, in actual fact, the briefing by 1 was by Sljivancanin or by Pavkovic? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. The -- who claimed responsibility of the hospital. What is the next reference that you have there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That responsibility was not given to him because JNA demanded from ICRC written agreement about full responsibility for hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just deal with that entry? The JNA demanded from the ICRC, namely Borsinger, the written agreement about the full responsibility for hospital. You -- you had, did you not, been involved with briefing and discussions about the evacuation and the evacuation document, the Raseta document?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any reference to that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. The two parties, it's in paragraph 7 of Raseta document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you be kind enough, please, to tell which tab you are on?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have used the tab 31, but Raseta documents is even in number 20, as I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's easier to use number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, the second sentence: "The two parties will also facilitate the involvement of the ICRC, Medecins sans Frontieres and the Maltese Cross, as appropriate, to allow them to play as much roles as may be decided in supporting and monitoring the evacuation." And paragraph 6 is: "The hospital will be put under the protection of the ICRC who will advise both parties of the period of neutrality which they require."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll deal with that in due course. Can I deal, before we move over the bridge, when you were in Vukovar, prior to the bridge and after the bridge, could you give the Court a description of the level of damage that existed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through Vukovar few times before war on my way to the coast-line, and it was a very nice, flourishing town, full of people. When we went there you -- you have heard what -- what I wrote down. There was no one single house which was not damaged at least roof. And what I remember well is a very small moment of the whole tragedy was that there was not one single branch of tree which can be untouched by a piece of shrapnel, so it shows the density of -- of shooting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at a sort video clip which was compiled in 1993. It has been disclosed to my learned friends. It's V0006642, it only lasts three minutes, less than that. I wonder, perhaps, if we could see that and see whether in actual fact this corresponds with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's what I saw. It's the water-tower in the centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Hotel Danube, and this is Vuka River we were standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would, in due course, make application to make that an exhibit. As I say, it was in 1993, I believe: I don't know if my learned friends have any objection to that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number 317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the first of the two videos of the meeting by the hospital, has that an exhibit number yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. The first one, the silent one with the transcripts, that was a 65 ter, 314 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you gave that reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But it does not have an exhibit number as such, and I would certainly make application for that to be an exhibit. Can I just indicate the slight -- it's not a difficulty, just not to complicate things. Exhibit 283 is the same video but extended round to show back down the road, but that doesn't have the transcript, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not a complication. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video clip will be exhibit number 318.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with the Vukovar Hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in very general terms, what you found when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the hospital there were some civil ambulances damaged. The entrance to the hospital was to the [indiscernible] or to the [indiscernible], because top or upper part of the hospital was under shelling and it was visible from outside. When we came down to the cellar we saw there if it was possible, because there was no light, light was provided by small bulbs from cars and by some accumulators [sic] from cars. People were lying on corridors and everywhere because there were few hundred, three to 400 people. In the -- in the cellar, cellar was connected with this -- some anti-nuclear or a bomb shelter. There were lying those heavily wounded people in the very centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we deal now, please, with the wounded people and their evacuation? So can we deal, then, please, with --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague and me, my colleague, Dr. Schou and me and Colonel Cunningham in the very beginning we were discussing the -- the question who should be removed first. Then we decided that probably the heavily wounded people should be the first one, because we were not sure that we have enough ambulances. So we decided to move the -- the heavily wounded as fast as possible from those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we deal, please, with page number 1403 in the handwritten copy?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is mentioned: "Bad organisation of loading patients to convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we just deal, whose job, whose responsibility was it to load patients?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According the agreement and the discussion before, we were told that JNA will -- will provide us with -- with personnel and with -- with ambulances and other support, and it is in agreement, I believe, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you just give a general description of how you saw the care or lack of care that was being used for the evacuation of patients?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people moving in -- in the -- the entrance of the -- to the hospital, so it was really difficult to go out, and then the problem with -- was that there was no one, or at least I couldn't see anybody who is the chief of -- of commanding this -- this evacuation. So sometimes I have to go for the driver of ambulance and said him, please, go to the entrance because we are waiting for another ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time personally attempt to assist in the loading?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, once I saw that one of those people who were carrying the stretchers was not strong enough and was tired probably, so I -- and the -- the patient could fell down, so I have -- I had help him in that case and move the -- the stretcher to the bus. I believe that it was to the bus, because some light wounded people, we were moving them to -- to buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did that have any reaction from anyone?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a reaction from one -- one man who was standing there, and he accused me that I am not impartial because I am helping the -- the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the ICRC representatives having an argument, and the ICRC, as far as you understood it, by way of the agreement, having the neutrality of the hospital was to be respected and the ICRC to be responsible. Is that right, in general terms, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- that -- this was written in -- in the information we got from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was written in the agreement of -- of Admiral -- of General Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to look at a video, 65 ter number 324. It is a video that -- clip that lasts four minutes. And it is of the ICRC representative at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could that be played? And there should also be a transcript to read just down below. And hopefully the sound will come through. Your Honour, again, there seems to be some problem with the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A technician will be here shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, may I just wait for the technician to arrive? Thank you very much. Your Honour, perhaps the best thing do is just to play it. There is a transcription down below, and we can play it a second time, if needs be, rather than waste time. Does that meet with the Court's agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like it to be heard, if possible. But the technician will see how long that will take. Well, we now have sound. I wonder if the Court would object to me playing it again with the sound. It's in English. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I make an application for that video and accompanying transcript to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 319.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, some of the phrases used there were that Nicholas Borsinger said that he was completely -- the ICRC were completely unable to carry out their task and that they had been prevented from entering the hospital. Were you aware at that time of the ICRC being restricted in their role in carrying out the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we know that they were not there. It was the only thing that I can remember, but -- I can't say. I can't say more, I can't remember more. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, just thinking a little harder, perhaps, in relation to the hospital, were you able to get into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were allowed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were free to move there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But within the hospital itself what did -- what function did you, the ECMM, actually perform?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We monitored the situation there, cease-fire existing, once we stopped the violation of neutrality of the hospital, because I was near the entrance and I have heard from the entrance some arguments, so I run down, and there was one volunteer with weapon, so I asked -- I don't know if it was liaison officer or some other officer, and they removed him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, in -- in the document that we have in front of us, the handwritten document, the second line says: "No visible action by the ICRC." And we clearly have seen that the video now. But it says: "Except arguments 6," clearly Borsinger, "with military representative." Is representative singular or representatives plural?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would you describe Nicholas Borsinger's approach and attitude at that time, his demeanour?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he was really unable to fulfill his task, because he -- as I have heard the -- the day before in the 19th, they were discussing that they will come - "they" means ICRC - will come in the evening to the hospital and that they will provide a list of patients and they did -- they will decide who has to be moved first and so on. So I was really surprised when I saw him in -- in our convoy when we were moving from -- from Negoslavci to -- to the -- to downtown, and then when we were in the hospital and we haven't got our list, and we have no contact with him, we have to do our best without him, because there were patients in the very dramatic situation, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Borsinger himself, how would you describe his -- his demeanour at that time? Do you understand what I mean by the word "demeanour?"

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: His attitude toward the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that we can see that on -- on the first footage, that he was not aggressive, but he was really trying to get an approach to the hospital and he was doing his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was trying to do his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And how would you describe the level of control of the JNA at the Vukovar Hospital? Or indeed prior to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say "full," can you be a little more expansive?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there with weaponry, with armoured carrier vehicles. High-rank officers were there. So it -- it was -- I think it was sovereign on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was on the territory, sorry?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sovereign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sovereign. Thank you very much. Can I ask you then about another entry. It's about six lines down. "Some patients asked me about ..."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Some patients asked me about the destiny of popular lady doctor Bosanac. I asked somebody from JNA not -- not liaison officer, neither some official person, and I was told non-official answer, 'she is Ustasha.'" But later we got the -- the official statement, I believe, that she was captured and she will be treated like war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can I just deal with the next line, it's ECTMS message?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No cease-fire on -- ECTMS means that it's a message coming from EC monitoring teams from the front line or crossing point. That: "There is no cease-fire on the front line and crossing points in Zidine since 1000 hours until 1500. After that, JNA decided to send convoy to Sremska Mitrovica for overnight care."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then I think it's right to say that eventually there was an evacuation, is that right, that day? Or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- can you repeat or reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm looking at f, and it says: "Decided to send convoy to Sremska Mitrovica for overnight care." And then the next entry is the SM barracks.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And of course you have in the first page of your entry arrival at the Sremska Mitrovica barracks at 5.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Having loaded the patients and others until 2.30?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So that's -- that's what I'm working on.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. So we went -- because there was no cease-fire on the crossing point, and we had that convoy with -- with those wounded people in a very bad condition, so JNA decided to -- to move convoy to Sremska Mitrovica barracks, where in the garrison there is even a small hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: You had been warned, apparently, at a briefing that if there are any soldiers, defenders on your convoy, the JNA couldn't guarantee your security?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they might get killed and you might get killed?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, here you have a convoy, and presumably there were some men on that convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, wounded men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how did you know whether any of those men, or indeed women, because it doesn't have to be a man, were not defenders of Vukovar and therefore putting your convoy at risk?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't care. They were wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you say you didn't care, you didn't care about what?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the danger. It was a responsibility of JNA, and so there was no question on security. It's a question of humanity. So we cannot go back to the hospital to those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so if in actual fact there had been a number of defenders on that convoy, would you still have taken that convoy out to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a question of -- of what -- what was better. And we -- we cannot change the -- the situation that was not -- there was no other or better possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I don't want to deal, really, with the rest of this particular entry. Perhaps if I -- in fairness, I think it's right to say that under g there's reference to: "Very good medical care provided at Sremska Mitrovica." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But prior to Sremska Mitrovica, what was the medical care like on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we took care about the convoy before -- before departure, only I was few times going there to see if ambulances or around ambulances is everything okay, if there are not crowds of people and so on. So it was okay. I know that Dr. Schou went to those ambulances as well to check people, and we were only two there and there were many hundred people, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We've got Dr. Schou coming next, so we can hear from him. Can we move to page 1404? And its comments, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comments, yes. "ECMM has no effective possibility of communications, what's dangerous. November 21st, we haven't any possible of contact with Belgrade or Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And number 2, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2: "Vukovar was destroyed by concentrated attack of all army means (artillery, air force, Danube - navy)," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The first line was provided mostly by Serbian volunteers and reservists. Destroying of Serbian villages in neighbourhood isn't compatible -- comparable, sorry. They totally destroyed Vukovar. Croat forces in Vukovar were probably much less than attackers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then I think there's two other reference that relates to the level of preparation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we were afraiding in the time that -- that the next town could have the same destiny, so there is an advice in number 3: "The next case of conquered town, probably Osijek, should be prepared for better care of civilian and wounded people in time." And 4: "It is necessary to manage some safety corridors for crossing front line (for refugees, wounded, prisoners of war, ECMM ... may be with permanent presence of ECMM."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so if I can leave it this way: With regard to the mandate that you had, namely you were to observe --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- but only complain at the end --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for the destiny of people who were -- who were removed before our arrival there, for instance, immediately on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you told that destiny or destination?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not concerning some of those people. Only -- only concerning Dr. Bosanac and some other from the top of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move on to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I make application for that to be made -- that document to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then may I briefly go to divider 25? At divider 25 appears to be a Vukovar relief mission, and that is ERN number 00381417 through to 1424. And the B/C/S is 03040385, 0304 through to 0391. I would like you just to look at this document, please. I don't wish to go into any considerable detail, but I would like to deal with one or two aspects of it. The first question is this: Who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is -- is made by the centre in Zagreb. I believe so, because there are mentioned even other teams which were not -- which were not under our responsibility from Belgrade, and you can see that it came to -- to Belgrade by fax. So the source is -- is probably somewhere else than in Belgrade. And if it is, then it has to be Zagreb. Headquarters of EC monitoring commission in Zagreb precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, in respect of this document I just want to deal with number 5. We have already dealt with 2, which is the agreement, I'm not going to repeat that. But can we deal with paragraph 5. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Reading, commencing "as it transpired"?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As it transpired, the convoy did not succeed on its first attempt following the failure of proposed cease-fire. Consequently the tripartheid meeting on the 20th agreed a new route from Sremska Mitrovica to Bosanski Samac and on to Djakovo through the following villages: Bijeljina, Brcko, Orasje."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know, not even from your personal knowledge but do you know from others, why it was it didn't succeed on the original route or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that there is no cease-fire on the front line. I don't remember because I was not there, and I had another problems in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, with the next page, 1418.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I want to deal, please, with 7 a (v)?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Much to the surprise"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Much to the surprise of the teams the handover was conducted at Dvorovi, a town 20 kilometres southwest of the transfer point."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say it was describing a Serbian village, ugly scenes developing at the transfer --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for translation. "Sick and wounded people took place. The teams witnessed aggressive chanting and violence towards drivers, medical staff and patients. The team decided in the circumstances to move the convoy as quickly as possible. As a result of the violence, one doctor and driver were badly beaten with buses and other vehicles damaged. See photograph in annex D."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then can we turn over to page 1419. It is b (i).

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 20th November" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we -- I don't think it's necessary to go that, although there is reference to whilst mines were cleared. But I think it's right to say you didn't know if mines were cleared; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were told. It's all the time the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to start halfway down the page: "On arrival at the hospital." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. "On arrival at the hospital, they found that JNA were in control and the International Red Cross, ICRC, are not been permitted entry to the hospital to begin the registration of sick and wounded. The hospital was described as overcrowded, some 300, 400 patients. It had been without water, electricity, medical supplies and food for two months."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Roman numeral (ii), can we deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Loading the sick, wounded and staff took until 1430 hours and was described as disorganised and chaotic, with no visible action by the ICRC apart from arguments with the military representatives. The majority of Croatian personnel did not wish to become involved in the loading of patients."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- and then finally, because it is something I'm sure that the Court will wish to deal with, 1422, I'd like to deal with observations, e. Now, this document, is it a compilation of various views?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when was this document compiled? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was compiled -- I am not able to say when. I'm trying to read the date from fax because it can be the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I think the fax just seems to be 12th, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th, so it's -- it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that's the date of the fax, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the date of the fax, so I don't know when it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we deal with e: "The ICRC must honour their role in accordance with any agreement, for humanitarian convoys and not become agitated and aggressive at the first sign of trouble." Now, in relation to that particular entry, as far as you are aware, was that particular clause generated because of the arguments with -- that Borsinger had with the JNA soldiers or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the outside it looks like aggressive, but if you follow the text, the context, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would seek to put this document in as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With exhibit number 321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to move, then, to document -- sorry, tab 26, and it is only one part of the document that I would wish to put before the Court. 26 is an English translation -- sorry, the English version is 00381425, ending in 1427, and the B/C/S is 03040115 through to 118. The part that I would seek to refer to, just by way of introduction, we have got the monitoring activity of the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this document, where -- what is the source of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an ECMM headquarters in Zagreb. It's a daily summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's a daily summary. And if we look top left-hand corner, can we see the date?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'd like you then to turn over, please, to page 1426. And I only want to deal with paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vukovar, whilst the teams were travelling from Belgrade to Vukovar, it was understood that the International Red Cross were in discussions with the new management of the hospital, i.e." --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "i.e., the JNA."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "i.e., the JNA. However, when the team arrived in Vukovar, they found that the JNA were running the operation. The International Red Cross has been ejected from the hospital at 2000 on the 19th of November. After receiving instructions from General Raseta, the registration process began, and the sick and wounded people were loaded into buses and ambulances."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to deal with -- here is the 19th, 2000 hours, 8.00 in the evening, and it's while the teams were travelling from Belgrade to Vukovar. Where did this information come that the ICRC had been actually been ejected at 8.00 on the Friday evening -- not the Friday evening, on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. It's what we have heard during -- during negotiation in Negoslavci, we have heard that ICRC wish is to -- to go there in the evening and to make their task, but I don't know from where the -- the information comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to make that document an exhibit, tab 26, but really in relation to paragraph 11, if it's possible to make a mark for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole document will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please? With regard to tab 29, that's already been made an exhibit, I believe. Taken out of sequence. I wonder perhaps if that could just be clarified. No, that hasn't. So I will just deal with it, if I may. Again it's part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 29, please. The document that I wish to deal with, part of it anyway, is the English translation is 00381433 through to 1436, with the B/C/S translation of the first two pages as 03033620 to 25, and then the English translation of 1436, the B/C/S translation there is 03029145. Now, can I deal, please, with the English, what appears to be the message form? Firstly the date appears to be the 21st of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time is 1 hour 23 minutes a.m., it means in the -- after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see it's actually on the top right-hand corner as well in the priority mark on it, to Split and Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the top being the evacuation of the wounded and refugees from Vukovar. Can I just deal, then, please, with the next page, which is 1434. It's number 4.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It appear to say liaison officer Belgrade, or office Belgrade. Can you read what is said?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my eyes it's really difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will try, and if I'm wrong my learned friends will correct me. "Please" -- something -- "of 60 wounded remaining in Vukovar Hospital. Also what has become of the staff. Are the ICRC involved?" Do you know what happened to the remaining wounded or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened to the staff?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what -- what happened to the wounded people, because when we went to Sremska Mitrovica hospital we were working there, Dr. Schou with patients there, and I was taking care about the rest of convoy, because part of convoy was situated in the sporting hall in the -- in the centre of the city, and the rest of convoy were -- were people who were sitting and sleeping in those buses there. So I have to go in each room in the hospital or to buses or to the hall to explain to them what is the reason why we have to -- had to move to Sremska Mitrovica hospital, why we are not on the crossing point, and so on. So we took care about them. Then I -- then Dr. Schou and me, we were sleeping there overnight, and in the early morning we went back to Vukovar to pick up the rest of wounded people, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the 20th we were not able to remove all -- or to evacuate all those -- all those people because there were no enough -- enough means for transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that when you arrived on the 20th you had been told by patients that there had been a group of people taken away before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went back on the 21st, were you ever told where that group of people were taken?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember in that very day the -- the situation in hospital was -- was very quiet, organised, so I believe that there was an interest to -- to evacuate those patients as soon as possible. What we did as a mission, we informed our -- our central in Zagreb, and then Zagreb has informed countries of European community and some other countries and they were trying, through international means, to release those people. I remember that there -- that in one such --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can leave it there and if there is to be any cross-examination about it, it can be done. But as far as you are aware, it was passed on, concerns were passed on to international organisations?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Can I deal, then, please, with one -- I think it should be the final document; I'm sure people would be glad to hear. It's tab 34. Now, can we deal with tab 34, please? It relates to a discussion with Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- it's a review of -- of the visit, because Belgrade centre was allowed to -- to visit her in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I just -- I'm not going to go through it all. But I want to deal, please, with the second page, and I'm sorry, I should have called out the details. 34 -- yes, it's ERN, English version, it's 00381406 through to 1409 as per the index. And the B/C/S is 03022809 through to 2812. Can we just deal then, please, in the English version with 1408? So it's the second page. My apologies, 10 -- sorry, 1407. So have we got 10 --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like you to go approximately two-fifths of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Told by EC on November the 19th." Have you got that entry?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Told EC on November the 19th convoy would be organised to evacuate hospital to Zagreb. No convoy on the 19th." Now, do you know or had you any dealings with any conversation that she had, the doctor had, with the EC about a potential convoy on the 19th? If you have no personal knowledge, please say so.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was -- it was my communication to her, through mobile phone. And I do have some probably some remarks in my notebook, if I can use it. Just a moment, please. Yes, it is the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1215 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written in Czech, and probably there is some excellent English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, to assist the Court, it's at 0468-7761. The translation version is 1 of 17, the bottom of that.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. So Dr. Bosanac said: "It was signed at the talks that ECMM would visit Vukovar Hospital by noon. I am asking you" -- she repeated it three times -- "to come as soon as possible. Situation in the hospital is dramatic. Red Cross couldn't come because they are shooting from the left bank." "They" means JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Again, if we just drop two lines down from that entry of divider 34, divider 34, not your hand one.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've got your hand on it, left hand. That's it.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Okay. So there is a cross actually at the document. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You don't know either, all right. "Command of JNA" --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Came without ICRC."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, again, the ICRC were supposed to be in charge of this evacuation and have the hospital isolated with the JNA not having access. Did you ask her about that or not? If you can't remember, do say so.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, number 34, divider 34, in the back of my memory, it's so long ago now, four or five months ago, I thought had been put to Dr. Bosanac, but if it has not, and has not been made an exhibit, I would seek to make divider 34 an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't answer your implied question, whether in a different form it was put. Certainly not as tab 34 of this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But before we deal with that, you did mean to tender tab 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I was not -- if my memory serves me correctly, I merely wanted to inquire about what had happened to the wounded of people on the 21st, but it just gave a completeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Tab 34 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And that concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Clearly this is a very convenient time for a break, resuming at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please, if you are ready, please continue, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kypr. First of all, I would like to introduce myself. My name is Miroslav Vasic, attorney-at-law. I am counsel for Mr. Mrksic. You understand the language I speak. That is at least my understanding, based on your testimony. I would still like to ask you to make a pause after each of my questions to allow for an accurate interpretation. After that please answer the question so that everybody can follow. Thank you very much, sir. You testified in chief about the role of the ECMM an organisation you belonged to in the autumn of 1991. You were on a mission there, and you made certain observations. Did you discuss this in 1996 with the OTP investigator, Vladimir Dzuro?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I -- if I may, I can go through my witness statement and I can find it there, if there is some observation. But if you ask me, I can tell you generally we were powerless. It was my observation about the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In actual fact, my question was more of a technical issue, whether you spoke to Mr. Dzuro, the ICTY investigator. I would like to know whether you spoke to anybody at the OTP back in 1996 and whether following any interviews a statement was drawn up that you signed in the presence of Mr. Dzuro. It's a technical detail that I would like to know about, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember. [In English] I do remember that. And it was written down in Czech version, which I do have. And it was translated to -- into English and I do believe to B/C/S as well. I found there some mistakes in translation. But yes, I did it, and it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to know for the time being. After giving this statement in 1998, on the 10th of February more specifically, you were summoned to give evidence before this Tribunal at a different trial related to Vukovar. This was the Dokmanovic case. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke to Mr. Dzuro you handed over a number of copies of ECMM reports that were in your possession?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of those interviews you learned that documents that were supposed to be at the -- kept at the regional centre of the ECMM based in Belgrade were no longer there, or at least were not available, or even that those documents had been destroyed, as well as the documents kept at the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb. Am I right in claiming that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I told to Mr. Dzuro that they can find those documents in files in Zagreb or in regional centre Belgrade, and I was told that there are only few, or I don't remember, so I was asked by Mr. Dzuro to provide him those documents I possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was my understanding too. In your statement you spoke about how you had obtained those copies and where those copies or documents had been kept before you got hold of them. What I want to know is whether Mr. Dzuro also managed to obtain some of these documents on that occasion, or are all the documents that we have in this binder in front of you documents that you obtained?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may go through, I saw there for instance, at least I remember one, and it is the copy of this Bapska ultimatum, as I do remember, or some of written hands document which came by fax, and I believe that it is not my copy. You can see that there is no my signature. It's in tab number 6. So it -- it is from another source, but maybe there are some others which are not coming from -- from mine -- from my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, sir, as to go through the binder and look at the documents? If could you please specify which are the ones that you obtained and which are the ones that were obtained from other sources, if that's not a problem, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So tab number 1, it is a part of my testimony -- not testimony, but witness statement, I believe. Yes, it is. 2 is as well as. 4 -- 3 is the organigramme of Belgrade centre, as well as it comes from my file. 4 is mine. 5 is mine. 6 is as well as from my file. I'm looking only on the first page, so maybe there are some other, but -- but the first page I confirm. I will go through the whole -- through the whole tab, if you wish. I will check each page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please check specific documents such as annexes, such as this Bapska ultimatum, which is attached to the document that you say you obtained. This is tab 6, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is tab 6. And there is one copy of -- of -- which comes from my documentation, and there is the other copy with the number 6919 at the end, and it is -- it comes from Industrogradnja Zabgreb fax, so it is -- it was from October the 15th, so it was sent from the headquarters of ECMM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about this handwritten document signed as -- on behalf of the JNA to the residents of Bapska? Is this something you obtained or did the OTP get this document from a different source? This is page 00381359 at tab 6. It should be just after that map.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, if I am looking at the -- this file, so the -- the first page says that with numbers 1353, that this is the report of team 7, Simons, Rodrigues, Martinez, from the 8th of October. And it says in the report that they got some -- some paper which is -- sorry, I have to go through to quote it in detail, if you wish. Yes, there on the page 1354, paragraph 3, the end of paragraph: "See annex C for example of an ultimatum." And you can see that there is annex C written. Originally it was A, and it was re -- it was fixed to C. So it is not my hand. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it was you who obtained the team 7 report, what I want to know is this: Did it have annex C attached to it or not, or did annex C come from elsewhere? That's what I want to know. Was this obtained by you or by someone else? If you can remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, and I made those copies as the files were, so if it is falsified, but I doubt, because it was in the -- in the documentation of -- of ECMM, so it's -- I can't see reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to tab 7, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's from my file.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one, please, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 8 is -- yes, it is from my statement, witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next one, please, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is from my file.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 10, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is from my file. If I see this -- those signatures on the paper it's visible that it is a part of this, if you can see those originals, so it's visible on the original, there is my signature and characters K-y, and in the case of tab 10 it is I-8. So it is symbol that it was a part of my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just in order to make this shorter, did I get this right: All the documents that were marked with a Y and a V or an L are documents that you obtained yourself? Am I right in that, sir, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a question, what do you mean obtained? I process this as copies, not -- I was not a member of those teams, let's say, or I was not in -- in each case I am not the author of that, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. I never said. But at one point when you gave that interview there was no documentation, you obtained some copies, some from your own files, some from the Czech foreign office files, and you said that some of the documents were actually obtained by the OTP investigator. What I want to know is: In view of the source of all these documents, which ones did you obtain and which ones came from other sources? That's why I'm asking you, the documents bearing your initials, are these documents which you personally obtained copies from a variety of sources just to save us going through all these documents. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. Correct is that all those documents which are presented there with those signatures and -- and symbols, Ky-I, are copies I obtained in EC Monitoring Mission, Belgrade centre, or in -- in Zagreb centre. So it is -- there is no any other source, neither Czech Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I have never said it. Neither Mr. Dzuro. If there is another resource, please put your question to the Prosecutor, because they provided the copy to the file only to show that there is another source for the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is much clearer now. You obtained copies of these documents. Thank you. Since the 1996 interview, do you know if any of the documents from the Belgrade headquarters and the Zagreb headquarters that were missing at the time have been found, the documents that were missing when the OTP were trying to track these documents down? Do you know anything about whether these documents have been found in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I was not in a contact with EC monitoring commission in Zagreb or in Belgrade since I left the -- the mission at the end of the -- December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a member of the mission do you perhaps have an opinion on this: How was it possible for some of the documents belonging to one of the regional headquarters of the ECMM to simply go missing, to disappear? Were you familiar with the rules for keeping these documents and filing them?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the regional centre Belgrade they were in a box, which was opened. And everybody from -- of each of monitors can go there, read reports which was sometimes necessary to -- to review the situation before, and so on. So everybody can go there to see it. So -- but I don't want speculate about how those things were stolen or destroyed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the lack of any original documents? Was that perhaps the reason that you placed your initials on each and every copy, as we can see? Just in order to show that the copy was faithful to the original, which at one time or another existed, and that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I am aware of, I was asked by Mr. Dzuro to make a signature on each document I am providing to -- as part of this witness statement. So I made my signatures on everything only to fulfill the -- the obligation. I was told that it is an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: By putting your signature there, did you mean to confirm the accuracy of these documents? Was that what you meant in actual fact by putting your signature there; namely, that these were documents from the ECMM archive as well as documents that you personally were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed that those documents I obtained, I copied, in ECMM archives. I cannot say that everything in those documents I can confirm with my signature, but the copies were in the -- were kept in such a manner that they cannot be, I don't know, replaced or something like that, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The documents that were produced by other teams working for the regional headquarters in Belgrade, had you ever seen any of those before you got copies of them in 1996 or was this the first time you saw them? Did you have an overview of any reports produced by other teams of which you were not a member?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to read about the work of -- of my colleagues, to get an -- to get an information in appropriate -- it was a security measure because I have to know how things are going. So we were reading that. Usually we were reading that when we were going to the place where other team had been before, so we have to read their reports and so on. So it was usual that we have to be aware of the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that the ECMM regional headquarters was set up sometime in September 1991, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. I believe so. I don't know exact -- exact date, but I know that I was sent the 16th of -- 15th or 16th I was sent from Zagreb, but I don't know when I came there and -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Belgrade and when the headquarters was set up, you were assigned liaison officers by the federal secretariat for All People's Defence. These liaison officers were meant to assist you with your tasks and duties, and you could also use them to get through to the federal secretariat for All People's Defence which was the army's supreme body, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we had several those liaison officers. I do remember two, Colonel Memisevic, and Major Zaric, I was working mostly with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You nearly guessed my next question. Colonel Memisevic was there an behalf of the federal secretariat for All People's Defence, and Captain Zaric was working as an interpreter at the time, as well as liaison officer. Was there somebody called Colonel Adam Loncar who was also working as a liaison officer at the time; do you remember him? He was assistant commander for moral guidance in the 1st Military District back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that after the headquarters were set up and after these liaison officers were assigned to you the federal secretariat for All People's Defence also set up a team to monitor any cease-fires and to monitor any activities by he ECMM? This team was headed by Lieutenant-General Nedeljko Maksimovic who was the deputy commander of the 1st Military District. Is this something you are aware of, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that and I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn or hear that there was a JNA body sending reports to the operations' headquarters of the federal secretary for All People's Defence, reports on your movements, on actions that were you taking or anything like that? Did any of the liaison officers that you were in touch with on a daily basis perhaps ever share something about this with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no any idea about that. What I can say that I saw only some passing formations coming about, but it was -- it was publicly sent to -- to -- as a -- as a press statement of JNA. So I have no knowledge about that we were, let's say, monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What about Lieutenant-General Nedeljko -- or Mladenko Maksimovic? I imagine you should know him because his name appears on the first page of your notebook 04087760. His name is right there. Did you know him in person or did you just simply write his name down in connection with this brief encounter that you described, the one that occurred on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his -- his name, his face. I don't know the reason why the name is there. If there is no contact, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you can, sir, please go to page 1 in your own notebook, just to avoid any confusion. This is 0468-7760. Right at the top of the page there is the name.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see the name. Yeah, I can see the name, that it was meeting with -- or he attended a meeting in Belgrade. It's all what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout your stint with the ECMM from September to December 1991, did you ever meet any representatives of the federal secretariat for All People's Defence or anybody from the General Staff of the JNA? Did you meet the commander of the 1st Military District, General Zivota Panic? Did you meet his deputy, Lieutenant-General Maksimovic. I see that there was a meeting. Did you meet these people or not? Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mission, or HOM, the head of mission and me as well, or Colonel Cunningham, we were meeting General Zivota Panic, as I remember. And what was the beginning of the question? Yeah, anybody from the General Staff or JNA. As you can see for me now, for my understanding now, MOD, Ministry of Defence, or Savezni Sekretarijat Za, is more a civil body, not -- civic body, not a military one. It seems that -- that I am -- I am wrong, because now I am living in this, and that people in uniforms, wearing uniforms were from both sides, not only from army and, but even from MOD or Savezni Sekretarijat. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The then concept of the structure of the federal secretariat for national defence, including the JNA General Staff, was quite different from the one which is enforced in contemporary systems. So in principle the federal -- at the head of the federal secretariat for national defence was General Veljko Kadijevic. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet with him or with Admiral Stane Brovet?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have met General Kadijevic, and I don't remember that I have met Admiral Brovet. Zivota Panic is another case. We were there few times, but not with those leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if you saw General Zivota Panic before your mission in Vukovar or afterwards, or both before and after?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we were asked by JNA or -- or MOD, "we" means mission, to come to Zivota Panic's office, because there is some violence [sic] of rules of memorandum of understanding or something like that. So we were asked to come as soon as possible. It was two days after Vukovar's fall. But then we recognised that the -- it was presented in -- on Serb TV like an example of excellent cooperation of ECMM with -- with military structures of Yugoslavia. So I don't know what was the main reason or real reason, and I don't want to speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday in response to my learned friend's question on a document in tab 6, which is Exhibit 305, you confirmed that this is a report drafted by team 7 of the observers from the regional centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when was the first time that you saw this report, including all the annexes that go with it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I had to read it before our teams went there, so as a member of -- of the team which is going there, we have -- have to read those -- those reports. But I don't remember that I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking, because I'm interested in these percentages of the ethnic composition of the population cited in paragraph 2, item 3 of the report. That's on page 00381353. You can see the percentages, the ethnic composition of the population in this region of Ilok. What I'm interested in is if you know where this information was received from about this ethnic composition. Do you have information where the team got its information from? Was it from the Croatian side or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about document which was written by somebody else, so I cannot tell you the source. I can only assume that -- that it was -- they were told by -- by Croats that -- about those figures. But I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to look at the document which is annex C to Exhibit 305, that's the document relating to the village of Bapska. Can you please tell me if you know how the team 7 got this annex C or this document?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The same answer that was written by them. And I don't remember if there is -- if there was some explanation referring to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that the tasks that you carried out as part of the European community observer mission, you saw a number of military documents. Does it seem to you that this document is a little bit odd? It's not in the usual format of the day, because it bears no stamp, it's written by hand, it was allegedly drafted in Sid on the 21st of September, 1991. So are you of the opinion that it's not in the form that it should be, in the form of a military document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question, because this witness is not qualified to give that answer, or indeed, is just being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether, Mr. Kypr, you are familiar with a military document so as to be able to describe or comment whether a particular document is in usual format or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember any military documents, only those press releases. And I don't remember. And some messages to us coming from -- from the very centre. So it is from Belgrade. This document supposed to be from the front line or from the -- from the field, so I can imagine that it can be written by hand, but I am really not an expert, so it's -- from my side, it is only speculation, both if it is not or if it is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we are not likely to get much further than that on that topic, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It's obvious that I didn't really do much or -- with this question, but thank you in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the -- this major, Bajraktarevic? Did you have the opportunity to meet such an officer in the Sid, Ilok or Backa Palanka area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen the content of this document, and my learned friend dealt with that on Friday. I'm interested in this name, Borislav Tomic. Do you know whether team 7 of the observer mission contacted this gentleman in order to check the contents of the document attached to the report? Do you have information like that, and is that something that is customary in the work of the observer mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no -- any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it the practice in the work of the monitoring mission to check through the sources for various documents, the actual contents of the documents?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if you were in the monitoring mission's team that visited the village of Brsadin on the 10th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the team comprised an observer who was from Czechoslovakia and also a person from the Netherlands, would that remind you? Were there any other observers from Czechoslovakia that were part of the European monitoring mission at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that time there were, I think, six, maybe eight. I don't know the exact number, but it was more than four members of ECMM coming from Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were they all part of the regional centre of the monitoring mission in Belgrade, or were they also in Zagreb, Sarajevo and other centres? In other words, how many of them were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade in that time I was the only Czech, or Czechoslovakian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, the village of Brsadin, according to the division at the time, division of tasks at the time, was it -- was it in the jurisdiction of your observer mission or monitoring mission from Belgrade, or was it under the jurisdiction of the one in Zagreb? Do you remember, was there any sort of rule there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but your answer was not recorded. Is it necessary for me to repeat my question? I will repeat the question. It will be easier --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which place or to which area of responsibility belongs Brsadin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you do not remember, that is the part that was omitted in this answer. The second part of the answer was recorded in the transcript. Thank you. Could you please turn to tab 12?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's document which, in B/C/S, has the number 00381387, and also 00381388. In English, in the English translation it's 03037649, 03037650. Mr. Kypr, you see this document. Is that the -- are those the minutes on the -- or the report on the referendum carried out in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
